42896449.label: Background
42896449.text: Lymph node metastasis identification has important clinical implications for treatment decision-making in rectal cancer (RC). To evaluate the diagnostic performance of the CT-based Node Reporting and Data System 1.0 (Node-RADS) for lymph node metastasis risk in treatment-naive RC patients, and to investigate the correlation between the Node-RADS score and clinicopathological factors.

42896449.label: Methods
42896449.text: A single-center retrospective study was performed to RC patients (Aug 2020-Dec 2025) who underwent radical resection surgery and preoperative contrast-enhanced CT examination. Lymph node status was assessed using Node-RADS score ranging from 1 to 5. Sensitivity, specificity, and Youden's index were calculated for different Node-RADS cut-off values. The overall diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curves and the area under the curve (AUC). The associations between Node-RADS score and clinicopathological parameters were analyzed.

42896449.label: Results
42896449.text: A total of 459 RC patients were evaluated, including 174 pN + and 285 pN-. Node-RADS scores ≥ 3 and ≥ 4 have the satisfactory diagnostic performance, with sensitivity/ specificity/Youden's index of 87.36 %/58.25 %/0.46 for Node-RADS scores ≥ 3 by Reader 1, 89.08 %/54.04 %/0.43 for Node-RADS scores ≥ 3 by Reader 2, 74.14 %/78.95 %/0.53 for Node-RADS scores ≥ 4 by Reader 1, and 72.99 %/75.44 %/0.48 for Node-RADS scores ≥ 4 by Reader 2, respectively. The AUC of Node-RADS scores were 0.831(95 %CI:0.793-0.864) and 0.806(95 %CI:0.767-0.841) by Reader 1 and Reader 2, respectively. Node-RADS score correlated with pathological T stage, N stage, and lymphovascular invasion. The inter-reader agreement for Node-RADS score were substantial, with weighted kappa values of 0.650.

42896449.label: Conclusions
42896449.text: The CT-based Node-RADS demonstrates stability and satisfactory diagnostic performance for identifying patients with lymph node metastasis in treatment-naive RC.

42911849.text: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension is a frequently debilitating condition that is most commonly caused by loss of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the spine. The most frequently occurring types of spontaneous spinal CSF leaks that cause spontaneous intracranial hypotension are ventral dural tears, lateral dural tears, and CSF venous fistulas, but other leak types are recognized including sacral dural tears or fistulas into vascular malformations. Localization and characterization of spinal CSF leaks with CT myelography facilitates subsequent targeted treatment. A tailored approach based on the suspected leak type as determined at MRI of the spine is necessary to maximize the likelihood of a diagnostic study. The authors focus primarily on advanced CT myelographic techniques for leaks from dural tears and CSF venous fistulas. The importance of optimal patient positioning, typical and atypical appearances of the different leak types, and artifacts that can mimic a CSF leak are considered.

42912649.text: A 71-year-old woman with a 5-week history of right-sided abdominal pain was initially suspected of hepatobiliary disorders. Upper abdominal ultrasound and MRI revealed unremarkable hepatobiliary findings. Although no hepatobiliary lesions were identified, MRI incidentally detected an ascending colon mass highly suspicious for malignancy. The patient underwent FDG PET/CT for differential diagnosis and preoperative staging. PET/CT with 3D CT reconstruction demonstrated a linear hyperdense foreign body within the ascending colon wall, causing focal bowel wall thickening with intense FDG avidity. These imaging findings were consistent with a foreign body-induced inflammatory granuloma, a diagnosis ultimately confirmed by colonoscopy and biopsy.

42957199.text: The incremental value of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT over multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) for selecting patients for prostate cancer focal therapy is undefined. Unlike lesion-detection studies, we evaluated whether PSMA PET/CT, mpMRI, and their combination correctly determine focal therapy eligibility when validated against whole-mount histopathology (WMHP). Methods: We retrospectively analyzed patients undergoing radical prostatectomy (RP) at UCLA (2017-2024) with preoperative PSMA PET/CT and mpMRI, a biopsy grade group (GG) of 3 or less, unilateral disease, and a prostate-specific antigen level of less than 20 ng/mL. Two blinded readers per modality assessed extraprostatic extension (EPE), seminal vesicle invasion (SVI), bilateral disease, and multifocality; a third adjudicated discordances. Eligibility required the absence of all 4. On WMHP, ineligibility was EPE, SVI, multifocal or bilateral disease with a contralateral or secondary GG of at least 2 nodules, or any GG greater than 3 focus at RP. Modalities were compared by McNemar tests. Results: Of 112 patients, 77 (69%) were ineligible on WMHP, including 19 (17%) with a GG greater than 3 focus at RP. Sensitivity and specificity were 53% and 54% for PET and 70% and 49% for mpMRI. Combined imaging improved sensitivity to 83% (P < 0.001 vs. PET; P = 0.002 vs. MRI) but reduced specificity to 26%. Per 100 patients at this prevalence, this would correctly identify approximately 9 additional ineligible patients while falsely excluding approximately 7 true candidates. mpMRI was more sensitive than PET for EPE (77% vs. 32%, P < 0.001), whereas PET was more specific (90% vs. 58%, P < 0.001). Combined imaging improved detection of multifocal (44% vs. 23%, P = 0.001) and bilateral disease (45% vs. 23%, P = 0.002) versus MRI alone. Conclusion: Adding PSMA PET/CT to mpMRI significantly improves sensitivity for exclusionary features, reflecting complementary molecular and anatomic information. However, combined imaging still misses a substantial proportion of adverse pathology, so imaging alone should not determine eligibility.

42981999.label: Objectives
42981999.text: To evaluate the diagnostic performance in abdominal low-kV (kilo-voltage) contrast-enhanced CT (CE-CT) of patients from the emergency department (ED) between venous-phase-only reading sessions and arterial-venous-phase reading sessions.

42981999.label: Methods
42981999.text: 96 patients (mean age 54 years, +/- 17, 49 men) who presented at the ED with undifferentiated abdominal pain underwent multiphasic low-kV CT including at least late arterial phase (LAP) and portal venous phase (PVP). Two reviewers, (Reader 1-board certified radiologist with subspecialization in gastrointestinal imaging and Reader 2-advanced resident with experience in gastrointestinal imaging), analyzed the PVP and LAP independently and determined the most appropriate diagnosis. LAP and PVP images were compared to a reference standard. Sensitivity, specificity and accuracy of the PVP for both readers were calculated. Incremental diagnostic value of the LAP was evaluated.

42981999.label: Results
42981999.text: The PVP showed sensitivity, specificity and accuracy in detecting relevant pathology of 93.2%, 87.5% and 92.7% in Reader 1 and 89.8%, 75.0% and 88.5% in Reader 2, respectively with concordant results in 85.4%. There were no findings exclusively detectable in the LAP relevant for clinical management, however it caused approximately 40% of the radiation dose.

42981999.label: Conclusion
42981999.text: PVP-only imaging with low-kV technique reduced radiation exposure while providing sufficient diagnostic information, suggesting selective use of additional arterial phase for a specific patient group with suspicious vascular emergencies.

43000449.label: Objectives
43000449.text: Patient-specific computed tomography (CT) phantoms can be produced using a novel 3D-printing technique that aims at replicating measured CT image volumes with high anatomic fidelity and accurate CT values. The purpose of this study is a comprehensive physics-based evaluation of both technical phantoms and a full-size adult abdominal phantom with regard to image-quality metrics and the reproducibility of CT values. In addition, the visualization of abdominal pathologies will be assessed.

43000449.label: Materials and methods
43000449.text: The study was conducted in 3 steps. First, a geometric reference disc phantom (40 mm thickness, 150 mm diameter) was 3D-printed using multimaterial jetting and scanned on a commercial photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT) to assess the CT values of the base materials used for printing and to evaluate the influence of the printing process on spatial resolution and noise properties. Second, CT images of the reference phantom reconstructed with a medium-sharp and a sharp kernel were used as templates to print 2 CT-derived disc phantoms using multimaterial jetting with voxel-based material mapping. These phantoms were then scanned to assess how template image sharpness propagates into the image-quality properties of the final printed phantoms. Spatial resolution was evaluated using edge spread function (ESF) analysis and edge rise distance (ERD), whereas noise characteristics were assessed using noise power spectrum (NPS) analysis. Third, as a proof of concept, a full-size adult abdominal phantom was 3D-printed with a patient CT data set as template. Phantom images were compared with patient images regarding CT values, spatial resolution, noise properties, and the depiction of pathologic structures.

43000449.label: Results
43000449.text: Evaluation of the CT attenuation of the base materials showed that CT values ranging from -37 HU to 995 HU in virtual monoenergetic images at 60 keV can be printed.For the reference disc, measured ESF curves showed close agreement with theoretical expectations across all reconstruction kernels, indicating preservation of spatial resolution by the printing process. CT-derived discs showed minor edge smoothing compared with the reference for smooth and medium-sharp reconstructions. For sharp reconstructions, edge smoothing was severe, with an ERD increase of up to 32% compared with the reference. Edge smoothing was more pronounced for the disc based on a sharp template. NPS were highly consistent across all discs, with only minor differences in peak amplitude. In the abdominal phantom images ESF and NPS closely matched those of the patient CT images. Measured attenuation agreed well for tissues with positive CT values up to 1000 HU. Fat was represented with increased CT values because of print material limitations. Clinically relevant pathologic structures, including a large hepatocellular carcinoma and a smaller focal liver lesion, were displayed comparably in the phantom images.

43000449.label: Conclusions
43000449.text: CT phantoms generated from CT image volumes using 3D printing with multimaterial mapping on a voxel level accurately reproduce the template images in terms of image sharpness, noise characteristics, and attenuation properties of tissues with positive CT values not exceeding 1000 HU. The achievable spatial resolution is limited to medium-sharp levels and does not improve by using sharper template images. These findings support the use of image-based multimaterial 3D printing to produce realistic anthropomorphic phantoms for advanced CT image-quality assessment and optimization, and for validation of reconstruction algorithms and quantitative CT imaging methods.

43018449.text: Purpose To identify accurate imaging protocols for energy-integrating detector (EID) CT and photon-counting detector (PCD) CT, to establish comparable protocols across systems, and to evaluate the reproducibility of lung densitometry across body sizes, sites, and dose levels. Materials and Methods A chest phantom and a multidiameter phantom were scanned across four academic medical centers with PCD CT and EID CT systems across three doses. PCD CT included standard-resolution and ultrahigh-resolution (UHR) acquisitions with low-energy threshold (T3D) and virtual monoenergetic image (VMI) reconstructions, whereas EID CT used filtered back projection. Soft and sharp body and quantitative kernels were evaluated. Optimal protocols minimized mean absolute error (MAE) from reference CT attenuation values. Comparable protocols were identified using the histogram similarity index (HSI) within the lung sample (chest phantom), and reproducibility was assessed using air-insert density measurements. Statistical analyses included a Gaussian linear mixed-effects model and nonparametric tests for reproducibility. Results PCD CT outperformed both EID CT systems (P < .05) across 7392 measurements, achieving a lower MAE (3.7 HU ± 3.7 [SD]) than EID CT1 (6.4 HU ± 4.0; P < .05) and EID CT2 (12.4 HU ± 9.7; P < .05). The optimal PCD CT protocol used the UHR mode, high-dose, standard-resolution VMI, and soft quantitative reconstructions. Protocol matching across scanners was feasible, yielding an HSI of 95.6% ± 1.2 under optimal settings. Compared with EID CT, PCD CT exhibited greater reproducibility across body sizes (<2.2 HU), across sites (<2.5 HU), across dose levels (<3.9 HU), and within dose levels (<2.5 HU). Conclusion PCD CT provided more accurate and reproducible lung densitometry while maintaining comparability with EID CT protocols.

43036949.text: 18F-FDG PET/MR demonstrated extensive right cerebral cortical hypometabolism in a 52-year-old man with Sturge-Weber syndrome undergoing presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy. Clinical photographs showed capillary malformations involving the face and both hands. CT revealed prominent right hemispheric gyriform calcifications, while integrated 18F-FDG PET/MR demonstrated ipsilateral cerebral atrophy and reduced cortical uptake in the frontoparietal and temporal lobes. These images illustrate the complementary roles of CT and 18F-FDG PET/MR in characterizing structural abnormalities and regional metabolic impairment in longstanding Sturge-Weber syndrome.

43070999.label: Purpose
43070999.text: This study aimed to evaluate the predictive and diagnostic value of baseline and post-treatment 18F-FDG PET/CT metabolic and structural features in distinguishing true residual tumor from immune-related inflammation in LA-NPC.

43070999.label: Methods
43070999.text: This single-center retrospective analysis enrolled 95 consecutive stage III-IVA LA-NPC patients receiving first-line neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy. All underwent pre- and post-treatment 18F-FDG PET/CT measuring metabolic parameters and structural features (extranodal extension [ENE]). Depth of metabolic response (DMR) was the primary endpoint; biopsy histopathology (n = 22) acted as gold standard. Multivariable regression, Spearman correlation, ROC-AUC with bootstrap validation, and sensitivity analyses were applied.

43070999.label: Results
43070999.text: Baseline SUVmax (OR = 1.146 [95% CI: 1.051, 1.250]; P = 0.002) and ENE (OR = 0.171 [95% CI: 0.054, 0.544]; P = 0.003) independently predicted poor and strong DMR, respectively. Patients with baseline ENE showed higher post-treatment EBV DNA non-clearance rates (34.1% vs. 9.8%; P = 0.008). In the biopsy subgroup with discordant biochemical-imaging status, true residue had higher baseline primary tumor TLG (P = 0.048) and ENE prevalence (80.0% vs. 16.7%; P = 0.028) than inflammation. A post-treatment nodal-dominant pattern (Post-T/N ratio ≤ 0.9) was associated with a lower rate of pathologically confirmed primary-tumour residue than a primary-dominant pattern (11.1% vs. 46.2%), negatively correlating with peak CRP (rho = -0.523, P = 0.012), indicating that nodal-dominant uptake accompanied a more intense systemic inflammatory response rather than residual disease.

43070999.label: Conclusion
43070999.text: In LA-NPC, baseline SUVmax and ENE independently predict neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy response. Combining baseline metabolic and nodal structural features distinguishes true residual disease from immune-related inflammation.

43073449.label: Background
43073449.text: [18 F]fluorocholine PET/CT is increasingly used for localization of hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue, but its real-world positioning after non-conclusive conventional imaging remains less clearly defined. This retrospective, observational, two-center study evaluated the use of [18 F]fluorocholine PET/CT as a second-level imaging modality in consecutive patients with suspected or biochemically confirmed primary hyperparathyroidism, within the Italian national reimbursement framework under Law 648/96.

43073449.label: Results
43073449.text: A total of 599 consecutive patients evaluated between February 2022 and July 2025 were included. [99 m]Tc-sestamibi imaging, with or without SPECT/CT, was positive/localizing in 270/599 patients (45.1%) and negative or doubtful/non-conclusive in 329/599 patients (54.9%). Overall, 132/599 patients (22.0%) underwent [18 F]fluorocholine PET/CT, all within the subgroup with negative or doubtful/non-conclusive sestamibi imaging, corresponding to 132/329 patients (40.1%). PET/CT was positive in 100/132 patients (75.8%) and negative in 32/132 patients (24.2%). Baseline PTH was significantly higher in PET-positive than in PET-negative patients: 118.8 (IQR 94.0-156.5) versus 105.0 (IQR 81.8-120.5), p = 0.012. Surgery was performed in 154/599 patients (25.7%) overall and was more frequent in PET-positive than in PET-negative patients: 41/100 (41.0%) versus 3/32 (9.4%), p < 0.001; OR 6.72, 95% CI 1.92-23.53. In exploratory multivariable analysis, PET/CT positivity remained independently associated with surgical management after adjustment for baseline PTH, serum calcium, age, and sex: adjusted OR 5.89, 95% CI 1.60-21.63, p = 0.008. Among patients with paired postoperative data, significant reductions were observed in PTH and serum calcium. Exploratory ROC analyses showed only modest discriminative ability of baseline PTH for imaging positivity.

43073449.label: Conclusions
43073449.text: In this large two-center real-world cohort, [18 F]fluorocholine PET/CT was selectively used as a second-level imaging modality in patients with primary hyperparathyroidism and negative or doubtful/non-conclusive [99 m]Tc-sestamibi imaging. PET-positive findings were associated with higher baseline PTH levels and subsequent surgical management, supporting the role of [18 F]fluorocholine PET/CT as a decision-supporting modality within the diagnostic pathway.
